question: to the Commission Giuseppe Antoci (The Left) Subject:

The problem of rising food prices over the past year remains an open issue, as shown by recent Eurostat data. This is despite the European Central Bank (ECB) forecasting food inflation to slow down in the coming months1. The issue weighs heaviest on the most economically fragile households in Sicily, Sardinia and southern Italy. With these large increases in unavoidable expenditure ongoing, the region is in danger of being rather exposed to any new energy and geopolitical shocks2. As Eurostat’s data show3, annual inflation in the euro area increased by 3 % over the last month compared with the previous month of March. Despite the inflationary slowdown of around 1.5 % in 2025, prices remain particularly high compared to the period before the Ukraine war in 2022, which also had persistent effects on food, leading to a considerable rise in ‘shopping basket’ prices. In view of the above: 1.
What steps will the Commission take to curb food inflation in the most vulnerable regions, particularly Sicily?
Considering the ECB’s analyses, does the Commission intend to adopt specific extraordinary measures for island regions?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (27.7.2026) As stipulated in Article 127 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union, the mandate of keeping inflation in check rests with the European System of Central Banks. The Commission and Member States support this endeavour with a coherent mix of fiscal and structural policies geared towards stimulating real economic growth without overheating demand. Member States have been alleviating the impact of the recent surge in imported energy prices on the most vulnerable households and firms, while stepping up action to boost energy autonomy. Within the AccelerateEU Package1, the Commission has adopted a State Aid Temporary Framework and committed to assist Member States to make maximum use of cohesion policy funds in order to support their decarbonisation efforts, through renewable energy deployment, energy efficiency and clean technology manufacturing. The EU’s agricultural, fisheries and trade policies also foster the supply of healthy and quality food at reasonable prices, while the cohesion policy helps to tackle possible bottlenecks in value chains, which may also help address increases in local prices. The Commission does not envisage adopting specific measures to curb food inflation in specific regions. It encourages Member States to mitigate the economic and social impact of the energy crisis with measures that are temporary, targeted and fiscally sustainable – particularly in countries with high public debt – and preserve the price incentive to reduce demand for fossil fuels.
